say: You give it the graphs of two functions, or one graph and a number. It finds the $x$ values where $f(x) = 0$, $f(x) = k$ or $f(x) = g(x)$, by reading them off the graph.
The key idea: an equation is a question about where two heights match. Draw the second height as a line or curve, and the answers are the $x$ values of the points where the two meet.

how.higher: Higher level uses it as a short part inside a longer Paper 1 or Paper 2 question: read where two plotted functions meet, or how long a tide stays above a level.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level tests it nearly every year on Paper 1, usually as a 5 or 10-mark part: read the roots, a value or a range of $x$ off a graph the question has already drawn or asked you to plot.

example.question: The graph of $f(x) = x^2 - 2x - 8$ is drawn for $-4 \le x \le 6$. Use the graph to estimate the values of $x$ for which $f(x) = 5$. Give your answers correct to one decimal place.

steps.title: Read the question as a height
steps.say: The equation $f(x) = \hl{1}{5}$ asks: where is the curve at height $\hl{1}{5}$?

lines.text: On the graph, find the points of the curve whose $y$ value is $\hl{1}{5}$.

steps.title: Draw a horizontal line
steps.say: Draw a horizontal line across the graph at $y = \hl{1}{5}$. Mark each point where it cuts the curve.

lines.text: The line cuts the curve in two places, so there are two answers.

steps.title: Read down to the x-axis
steps.say: From each point, go straight down to the $x$-axis and read the value.

steps.title: Check by algebra
steps.say: Put the equation equal to zero and solve it. The answers should agree with your readings.

lines.text: The formula gives $x = 1 \pm \sqrt{14}$, which is $\hl{2}{-2.7}$ and $\hl{2}{4.7}$.

higher.tip: Mark the intersection on the graph itself. The marks are tied to it, even when the value of $x$ is not stated.

sources.quote: Point of intersection indicated on graph

higher.tip: Values read from a graph are accepted within a tolerance, so read carefully but do not over-polish.
A clearly marked intersection earns partial credit on its own.

sources.quote: point of intersection clearly indicated on

ordinary.tip: Show your work on the graph. Relevant work on the graph earns partial credit even when the value you read is off.
Do not give just the answers. Correct answers with no work on the graph lose marks.

sources.quote: Both answers correct but no work

ordinary.tip: When one answer builds on the last, keep them consistent. A bare answer in a later part must match your earlier reading.

sources.quote: must be consistent with answer from (i)

ordinary.tip: When asked how many roots, give the reason from the graph: how many times it cuts the $x$-axis.

say: You give it two functions, $f$ and $g$. It finds where they are **equal**, and the ranges of $x$ where one graph is above the other.
The key idea: the two graphs meet exactly where $f(x) = g(x)$. Between those meeting points, one graph stays above the other, so one test value tells you which.

how.higher: Higher level uses it inside bigger questions on Paper 1: set the functions equal to find the meeting points, then use them as limits for an area or to judge which function is larger.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it as a part of a Paper 1 question: read where two plotted graphs meet, say which is cheaper or larger, or find the range of $x$ where one is below the other.

example.question: Let $f(x) = x^2$ and $g(x) = 2x + 3$. Find the values of $x$ for which $f(x) = g(x)$. Hence state the values of $x$ for which $f(x) < g(x)$.

steps.title: Set the functions equal
steps.say: The graphs meet where $f(x) = g(x)$. Write that as an equation and move everything to one side.

steps.title: Factorise and solve
steps.say: Factorise. Each bracket can be zero, so $\hl{1}{x}$ has two values.

steps.title: Test between the meeting points
steps.say: The graphs cross at $\hl{1}{-1}$ and $\hl{1}{3}$, so one is above the other all the way between them. Test one value in that gap.

lines.text: So $f$ is below $g$ between the meeting points.

steps.title: State the range
steps.say: Use strict inequalities. At the meeting points the two are equal, not less.

higher.tip: Start by writing $f(x) = g(x)$ as an equation. That step has marks of its own.
If you can, check one answer by substituting it back. The scheme lists a verified answer as high partial credit.
Factorise the equation fully. A fully factorised equation is a stage with marks.

ordinary.tip: Write the equation that sets the two functions equal. A correct equation earns credit before any solving.
When asked for a range of $x$, use strict inequalities. Including the end points where the functions are equal loses a mark.
When you say which graph is larger or cheaper, give the reason too. An answer with no reason earns only partial credit.

sources.quote: B given as answer but no reason

say: You give it a function with its domain and codomain. It tells you whether the function is **injective**, **surjective**, both (**bijective**), or neither, and gives the reason.
The key idea: injective means no two inputs share an output. Surjective means every element of the codomain gets hit. A function that is both has an inverse.

how.higher: Higher level tests it on Paper 1 as a part of a function question: 5 marks to show a function is bijective and find its inverse (2016), and 10 marks to explain why a mapping between sets is injective but not surjective (2023).

example.question: The function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined by $f(x) = 7 - 2x$. Show that $f$ is bijective.

steps.title: Test injective
steps.say: Injective means two inputs with the same output must be equal. Take two inputs $a$ and $b$ with $f(a) = f(b)$ and see what that forces.

steps.title: Solve for x in terms of y
steps.say: Surjective means every $y$ in the codomain is an output. Take any $y$ and try to solve $y = f(x)$ for $\hl{1}{x}$.

steps.title: Check it is hit
steps.say: For every real $y$, $\hl{1}{\tfrac{7 - y}{2}}$ is a real number, so it is in the domain. Put it into $f$ to confirm it gives $y$.

lines.text: So $f$ is **surjective**. It is injective and surjective, so it is bijective.

workedSolution.finalAnswer: f \ \text{is injective and surjective, so bijective}

higher.tip: To show injective, say no element of the codomain is used more than once. Any valid reason is accepted.

sources.quote: no element of C is used more

higher.tip: To show not surjective, compare the range with the codomain: if they differ, it is not surjective.
A function is bijective if its inverse exists. Writing that, or $f^{-1}$, earns marks.

sources.quote: Function is bijective if inverse exists

higher.tip: The horizontal line test is an accepted way to show a function is injective.

say: You give it a function $f(x)$ and a transformation, such as $f(x) + k$, $f(x + h)$ or $kf(x)$. It gives the new graph or its equation.

The key idea: a change **outside** the brackets moves or stretches the graph up and down. A change **inside** the brackets acts on $x$, so it works sideways and backwards: $f(x - 2)$ moves the graph two to the **right**.

how.higher: Higher level uses it on Paper 1 as a short part: sketch the image of a given graph after a shift (10 marks), or substitute $0.8x$ into a cubic to model a stretch (5 marks).
how.ordinary: Ordinary level uses it as a step in a Paper 1 question: add a number to a function value, or plot a shifted copy of a graph from a table of values.

example.question: Let $f(x) = x^2 - 3x$. The graph of $f$ is moved 2 units to the right and then 4 units up. Write the equation of the new graph, $g(x)$, in the form $x^2 + bx + c$.

steps.title: Move right by 2
steps.say: A move of 2 to the right replaces every $x$ with $\hl{1}{x - 2}$. It acts inside the brackets, so it works the opposite way to what you expect.

steps.title: Expand and simplify
steps.say: Multiply out both brackets, then collect like terms.

steps.title: Move up by 4
steps.say: A move up of 4 adds $\hl{2}{4}$ to the whole function. It acts outside the brackets, so it does what you expect.

higher.tip: Transform a few key points of the graph and plot them. One point correctly transformed earns partial credit.
Write the transformation in terms of the original function first, for example $h(x) + 15$. That alone is work of merit.
For a stretch like $0.8x$, replace every $x$ and then expand. Starting the substitution earns partial credit.
If the question is in radians, give the period in radians. A period in degrees costs a mark.

ordinary.tip: When you shift a plotted graph, plot every shifted point and join them. One point wrong, or no joining, costs a mark.

sources.quote: Apply a * if one point plotted

ordinary.tip: Build a table of values for the new function. Three correct entries earn high partial credit.

sources.quote: Three correct points or table entries
